Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-26
Time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Cole (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Jonah Reyes (Redwood CSM); Nina Patel (Mortar Head of Platform), Roberto Diaz (SRE), Lena Kim (Product), Samir Voss (Security), Anya Chen (Engineer)

Summary (auto):
Mortar recapped a recent production degradation that caused long tail latencies during a night batch. Redwood and Mortar aligned on immediate mitigations (canary on staging, enable prefix caching, tweak batch windows), confirmed security/compliance constraints for logs, and agreed to a runbook rehearsal and shared benchmarks. Action items assigned; next step is a joint canary and runbook rehearsal.

- Evidence from logs and traces (KV cache thrash, GPU OOM, spike in long-tail user prompts)

- Scheduling a runbook rehearsal and next validation steps

--- Transcript body (partial, auto-generated, imperfect) ---
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood AE): Hey folks, thanks for joining, we'll try to keep this focused — we have Maya and Jonah on from Redwood. Nina, do you want to kick off with a one-sentence summary of what happened?
[00:15] Nina (Mortar): Yeah thanks, so overnight on Tue around 02:10 UTC we saw a tail latency surge on inference for the clinical-summary route, some requests were hitting 10s instead of the usual 0.8 to 1.2s. We had partial fallbacks to a smaller model but that introduced quality regressions.
[00:35] Roberto (SRE): For context, we were running Redwood Dedicatd pool — sorry, Redwood Dedicated — with a mix of quantized 8-bit and a 16-bit for the long prompts. We saw repeated cache misses in K-V cash, which caused repeated KV loads and GPU thrash.
[00:55] Maya (Redwood SE): Got it. A couple clarifying q's: when you say KV cache misses, is it prefix KV or full KV eviction during the run?
[01:10] Roberto: Looks like both; big sequence-length variance combined with a burst of few-shot prompts evicted prefixes. Also we hit a soar of peak tokens after a marketing campaign — probably correlated.
[01:28] Lena (Product): The marketing team sent a prompt template with multiple examples which increased sequence lengths; we didn't expect that distribution shift.
[01:40] Ethan: That matches what we see in the traces you shared — lots of cache churn. Our runtime logs show higher KV cache latency around the same timestamps, and a handful of worker restarts.
[01:55] Samir (Security): Quick note — the crash logs we shared are redacted. We need to keep PII out; we also need evidence retention to meet our audit window. Can you confirm Redwood won't request raw user payloads?
[02:08] Jonah (Redwood CSM): Yes, we agreed earlier to ingest only anonymized traces and index keys; we'll keep PII out of the artifacts. We'll document that in the runbook.
[02:20] Anya (Dev): One oddity: the fallback routing sent traffic to a smaller model variant that wasn't compatible with our post-processing — so we had malformed outputs and downstream failures.
[02:34] Maya: That's... not great. Our routing policies can be configured to fallback to model variants that guarantee schema compatibility; looks like the current policy used an unconstrained fallback and that caused the format mismatch.
[02:47] Roberto: Right, the policy default allowed any compatible signature, not schema.
[02:54] Ethan: Okay, immediate mitigations — we can push a config that restricts fallbacks to model-family X and ensures schema enforcement. We can also temporarily pin the route to the lower latency variant during the window while we test.
[03:10] Nina: Preference is to avoid user-visible regressions. If we can route to a dedicated pool with warmed KV caches, that's preferred. But we need to understand cost impact.
[03:22] Maya: Cost tradeoff: warming prefix caches costs tokens and compute. For a small window, Dedicated with prewarmed contexts will reduce tail latency substantially — we can share a cost estimate.
[03:35] Ethan: I'll share ballpark numbers today.
[03:38] [04:02] (crosstalk and brief hold music)
[04:10] Maya: Two short-term actions: 1) restrict fallback policy to schema-compatible variants; 2) enable prefix caching and increase TTL for the clinical-summary route in staging and run a canary.
[04:26] Roberto: For TTL, what's realistic? We don't want cache to grow unbounded.
[04:33] Maya: Start with 10 minutes for the canary; we can observe hit-rate and evictions.
[04:39] Nina: Also want to test with quantization profile 0.6 — we've been using 0.45 in prod to save cost but that may be amplifying memory pressure.
[04:50] Maya: 0.6 will use slightly more memory but better stability; we recommended 0.6 in our notes.
[05:02] Ethan: On the subject of kernel selection: our runtime picks kernels based on sequence length distribution. If the distribution shifts, kernel mismatches can cause suboptimal memory footprints. We can log kernel metrics to spot that in future.
[05:17] Roberto: We did see one or two OOMs on the worker where the memory allocation spiked.
[05:24] Maya: We'll also enable earlier OOM guards and slower shed — decrease batch window for the clinical route during peak hours so batch build-up doesn't cause memory spikes.
[05:35] Lena: How fast can those config changes be pushed to prod?
[05:40] Ethan: We can push config to staging today; prod requires a canary run. With the Dedicated pool changes it might be a few hours to schedule but we can prioritize.
[05:50] Nina: We want a formal runbook rehearsal. Not just a doc — walk through the steps with SRE + Redwood run the canary and failover.
[06:00] Jonah: We'll set up a 2-hour rehearsal. Proposed week of 2027-12-06.
[06:07] Samir: Security checks — we need to ensure KMS keys used for ephemeral clusters are rotated and listed in the audit. Also SOC2 evidence for the config push.
[06:20] Ethan: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; for Hosted we can provide per-tenant CMKs through the integration. We'll include the KMS audit snippet in the shared docs.
[06:33] Samir: Also, log retention — we need 365-day audit logs for the production cluster events. Is that supported?
[06:40] Jonah: We have an advanced observability add-on that supports longer retention and per-token cost breakdowns; we'll share the plan and cost.
[06:52] Roberto: A technical deep-dive question: could the batching window be the main culprit? We saw a pulse of requests at 02:09 which fell into a narrow window and inflated batch sizes.
[07:05] Maya: Yes. Continuous batching improves efficiency but is sensitive to request bursts. For this route, it's worth lowering max batch size and using a smaller max wait time for peak hours.
[07:15] Anya: Is there a way to route high-variance prompts to a separate pool automatically?
[07:21] Maya: Yes via smart routing policies — route by input length or by a pretrained classifier that tags requests as 'long' — then send longs to a pool with larger memory configs.
[07:33] Nina: We'll need to instrument that classifier and ensure it doesn't add latency.
[07:39] Ethan: the classifier can run as a lightweight prefilter — few ms — it's a tradeoff but recommended for production when variance is high.
[07:48] Lena: On the client side we can also limit example templates or chunk them; product will enforce guardrails for marketing.
[07:57] Roberto: Another item — the fallback variant used had slightly different tokenization behavior, leading to format changes. How do we ensure compatibility across variants?
[08:08] Maya: Model family pinning plus schema assertions on the API response. Redwood's function-calling / structured output support can enforce that.
[08:18] Samir: For compliance, we want structured logs for every fallback event with a reason code.
[08:25] Jonah: We'll add reason-code emission as part of the runbook steps.
[08:32] [08:50] (brief pause)
[08:55] Ethan: Let's capture the immediate mitigations and medium-term fixes: immediate = restrict fallback schema, set TTL 10m in staging, canary quantization 0.6, lower batch window; medium = classifier routing, prewarming dedicated pool for the route, increase observability retention.
[09:14] Nina: And we need steps for rollback — in case the canary fails we want to flip to a safe, slower path without user-visible errors.
[09:24] Maya: We'll prepare an automated failover that routes to a golden model variant with schema guarantees and returns a cached earlier response if available as a degraded mode.
[09:37] Anya: Caching earlier response — is that acceptable for some clinical workflows?
[09:42] Lena: For non-critical predictions yes, but for things that affect patient instructions we need fresh inference; product will tag routes as cacheable or not.
[09:54] Ethan: Good. Now let's nail down what Redwood will deliver by Monday: benchmark spreadsheet with before/after numbers, suggested kernel and quantization profiles, and a config diff for the staging TTL change.
[10:08] Maya: I'll prepare the spreadsheet — trimmed to the clinical-summary route — and include suggested gating thresholds and failure modes.
[10:16] Jonah: I'll produce the runbook draft and incident timeline and drop in the shared Drive.
[10:23] Roberto: We'll provision the staging cluster and load the canary dataset.
[10:29] Nina: Also want a small smoke test for downstream post-processing.
[10:33] Ethan: We'll coordinate — Redwood will supply sample traffic generator and expected outputs.
[10:39] Samir: Security wrap-up: provide the KMS audit snippet, list of roles with access to staging. We'll set an NDA annex for the logs for the rehearsal.
[10:50] Jonah: Noted.
[11:00] [11:15] (wrap-up and quick recap)
[11:20] Ethan: Recap: Redwood to share benchmark and config diffs; Mortar to provision staging and run canary; schedule 2-hour rehearsal week of 2027-12-06; action items in the doc.
[11:36] Nina: Thanks, appreciate the quick coordination.
[11:40] Maya: We'll aim to have the artifacts by Monday EOD.
[11:45] Lena: Thanks everyone.
